buckets.title: Vibe coding vocabulary
buckets.description: Plain-English dev words that help non-engineers prompt clearly and ship with AI.

terms.title: Repository (repo)
terms.shortDescription: The home folder for all your project's code and its full history.
terms.definition: A repository stores every file in your project plus a timeline of changes, so you can see what changed, when, and roll back if needed.
terms.whenToUse: Whenever you start a project or tell an AI assistant where the code lives.
aiPhrases: Set up a new Git repository for this project and explain what each generated file does.
examples: A GitHub repo named vibe-guide holding your app code and README.

terms.title: Commit
terms.shortDescription: A saved snapshot of your changes with a short note describing them.
terms.definition: A commit records the current state of your files plus a message, creating a restore point you can return to later.
terms.whenToUse: Each time you finish a small change that works and you want to keep it.
aiPhrases: Write a clear commit message summarizing the change I just made.
examples: "Add contact form validation" as a commit message.

terms.title: Branch
terms.shortDescription: A parallel copy of the project where you can try ideas safely.
terms.definition: A branch lets you experiment without touching the main version; you merge it back only once it works.
terms.whenToUse: Before attempting a risky change or starting a new feature.
aiPhrases: Create a new branch for this experiment so the main version stays safe.
examples: Working on "add-dark-mode" while "main" stays stable.

terms.title: Pull request (PR)
terms.shortDescription: A proposal to merge your branch's changes, open for review first.
terms.definition: A pull request bundles your changes so you or others can review, comment, and approve before they join the main project.
terms.whenToUse: When a branch is ready and you want a checkpoint or review before merging.
aiPhrases: Summarize the changes on this branch into a pull request description.
examples: Opening a PR titled "Add dark mode toggle" for review.

terms.title: Environment variable
terms.shortDescription: A setting or secret stored outside your code, like an API key.
terms.definition: Environment variables hold values that change per environment or must stay private, so secrets never live inside your code.
terms.whenToUse: Whenever you handle passwords, API keys, or settings that differ between local and live.
aiPhrases: Move this API key into an environment variable and show me how to reference it.
examples: Storing OPENAI_API_KEY in a .env file instead of in the code.

terms.title: API
terms.shortDescription: A doorway one app uses to request data or actions from another.
terms.definition: An API (application programming interface) defines how programs talk to each other—what you can ask for and what you get back.
terms.whenToUse: Any time you connect your project to an outside service.
aiPhrases: Explain what this API expects and write the call to fetch the data I need.
examples: Calling a weather API to show today's forecast.

terms.title: Dependency
terms.shortDescription: An outside package your project relies on to work.
terms.definition: A dependency is third-party code you install and build on top of; updating or removing it can change how your app behaves.
terms.whenToUse: When adding a library, or when something breaks right after an update.
aiPhrases: List this project's dependencies and explain what each one does in plain terms.
examples: Next.js and React are dependencies of this app.

terms.title: Deploy (ship)
terms.shortDescription: Push your project live so other people can actually use it.
terms.definition: Deploying takes the version on your machine and makes it available on the internet at a real URL.
terms.whenToUse: When a change is ready to go from "works for me" to publicly live.
aiPhrases: Walk me through deploying this project and what to check before going live.
examples: Deploying to Vercel so the site is reachable at a public URL.

terms.title: Frontend & backend
terms.shortDescription: The part users see versus the part that runs behind the scenes.
terms.definition: The frontend is the visible interface in the browser; the backend handles data, logic, and storage the user never sees directly.
terms.whenToUse: When pointing an AI assistant at the right layer of a problem.
aiPhrases: Is this a frontend or backend problem, and which file should I change?
examples: A button's look is frontend; saving the form to a database is backend.

terms.title: State
terms.shortDescription: The current data an app is holding in memory right now.
terms.definition: State is what the app currently "remembers"—like which tab is open or what a user typed—and changing it updates what's shown.
terms.whenToUse: When something "forgets" what you did or doesn't update on screen.
aiPhrases: Why isn't this updating on screen—walk me through the state involved.
examples: A checkbox staying checked is stored in state.

terms.title: Refactor
terms.shortDescription: Rewrite code to be cleaner without changing what it does.
terms.definition: Refactoring improves the structure or readability of code while keeping its behavior identical.
terms.whenToUse: When code works but is messy, or before building on top of it.
aiPhrases: Refactor this for readability and keep the behavior exactly the same.
examples: Splitting one giant function into smaller, clearly named ones.

terms.title: Edge case
terms.shortDescription: An unusual input or situation that breaks normal assumptions.
terms.definition: An edge case is a rare or extreme scenario—empty input, huge numbers, no internet—that code often forgets to handle.
terms.whenToUse: When reviewing a feature for what could go wrong.
aiPhrases: What edge cases am I missing in this feature, and how should I handle them?
examples: A form that breaks when the name field is left blank.

buckets.title: Working-with-AI words
buckets.description: The words that make you fluent at directing AI coding tools.

terms.title: Prompt
terms.shortDescription: The instructions you give an AI to get what you want.
terms.definition: A prompt is the request you write for an AI assistant; clearer, more specific prompts produce better results.
terms.whenToUse: Every time you ask an AI to write, change, or explain something.
aiPhrases: Rewrite my request as a clearer prompt that spells out the goal, constraints, and format.
examples: "Add validation to this form, keep the styling, and explain what you changed."

terms.title: Token
terms.shortDescription: The small chunk of text an AI reads and writes in.
terms.definition: AI models process text in tokens (roughly word-pieces) and bill and limit work by token count, not by character.
terms.whenToUse: When you hit length limits or want to understand cost.
aiPhrases: Is this prompt too long? Trim it to use fewer tokens without losing the key details.
examples: A long word like "hamburger" can be two or three tokens.

terms.title: Context window
terms.shortDescription: How much the AI can "hold in its head" at once.
terms.definition: The context window is the total text (your prompt plus its reply) a model can consider at one time; beyond it, earlier details get dropped.
terms.whenToUse: When the AI seems to "forget" something you said earlier.
aiPhrases: Remind me what's in your context now, and what you may have lost from earlier.
examples: Pasting a huge file can crowd out your actual question.

terms.title: Model
terms.shortDescription: The specific AI brain you're using—a tool with a name and version.
terms.definition: A model is a trained AI system; different models and versions vary in capability, speed, and cost.
terms.whenToUse: When choosing which AI to use, or understanding why results differ.
aiPhrases: Which model is best for this task, and what are the tradeoffs in speed and quality?
examples: A faster model for quick edits, a stronger one for hard problems.

terms.title: Hallucination
terms.shortDescription: When an AI states something false with full confidence.
terms.definition: A hallucination is AI output that sounds right but isn't—made-up facts, functions, or APIs that don't exist.
terms.whenToUse: Whenever you rely on AI output you can't yet verify.
aiPhrases: Flag anything in this answer you're unsure about so I can verify it.
examples: The AI "cites" a library function that was never real.

terms.title: Agent
terms.shortDescription: An AI that can take steps and use tools on its own, not just chat.
terms.definition: An agent is an AI set up to act—run commands, edit files, call tools—pursuing a goal across multiple steps with less hand-holding.
terms.whenToUse: When you want AI to carry out a task, not just answer a question.
aiPhrases: Act as an agent: plan the steps to build this feature, then do them one at a time.
examples: An AI that edits files, runs the build, and fixes errors in a loop.

buckets.title: Debugging words
buckets.description: The vocabulary that turns a scary error into a solvable puzzle.

terms.title: Error message
terms.shortDescription: The app telling you what went wrong, in its own words.
terms.definition: An error message is the text a program shows when something fails; it usually names the problem and where it happened.
terms.whenToUse: The first thing to read—before guessing—when something breaks.
aiPhrases: Here's the full error message. Explain in plain English what it means and the likely cause.
examples: "TypeError: cannot read property 'name' of undefined."

terms.title: Stack trace
terms.shortDescription: The trail showing exactly where an error happened in the code.
terms.definition: A stack trace lists the chain of calls leading to an error, with file names and line numbers—read it top-down for the source.
terms.whenToUse: When the error message alone isn't enough to locate the problem.
aiPhrases: Read this stack trace and tell me which file and line I should look at first.
examples: A list of files and lines ending at the one that actually failed.

terms.title: Log
terms.shortDescription: A running diary the app writes about what it's doing.
terms.definition: Logs are messages a program records as it runs, useful for seeing what happened right before something broke.
terms.whenToUse: When a bug doesn't crash but behaves wrong, or to confirm what ran.
aiPhrases: Add log messages around this code so I can see what values it's actually using.
examples: A server log showing each request and any warnings.

terms.title: Null / undefined
terms.shortDescription: A box that's empty when the code expected something inside.
terms.definition: Null and undefined both mean "no value here"; many bugs happen when code uses something that turned out to be empty.
terms.whenToUse: When errors mention "undefined" or "null."
aiPhrases: This is undefined when I expected a value—trace back where it should have been set.
examples: Reading user.name before the user has loaded.

terms.title: Status code
terms.shortDescription: A 3-digit number a server returns to say how a request went.
terms.definition: HTTP status codes report outcomes: 200 is success, 404 not found, 500 server error—the first digit signals the category.
terms.whenToUse: When a page or API call fails and you see a number.
aiPhrases: I'm getting a 500 on this request—what does that point to and how do I narrow it down?
examples: 404 means the address wasn't found; 500 means the server errored.

terms.title: Reproduce
terms.shortDescription: Making the bug happen again on purpose, reliably.
terms.definition: Reproducing a bug means finding the exact steps that trigger it—the first move toward fixing it.
terms.whenToUse: Before attempting any fix; you can't confirm a fix you can't trigger.
aiPhrases: Help me find the smallest set of steps that reliably reproduces this bug.
examples: "It breaks every time I submit the form with an empty email."

buckets.title: Shipping words
buckets.description: What you need to know to put your work live without fear.

terms.title: Production vs. local
terms.shortDescription: The live version everyone uses vs. the private one on your machine.
terms.definition: "Local" is the app running just for you while you build; "production" is the live deployment real users hit—and the two can behave differently.
terms.whenToUse: When something works for you but not live, or the reverse.
aiPhrases: This works locally but breaks in production—what differences usually cause that?
examples: A missing env var that exists locally but not on the live server.

terms.title: Environment
terms.shortDescription: A named setup where your app runs (local, staging, production).
terms.definition: An environment is a configured place your app runs, each with its own settings and data, so you can test safely before going live.
terms.whenToUse: When separating safe testing from the real, live app.
aiPhrases: Set up a staging environment so I can test changes before they hit real users.
examples: Staging mirrors production but with test data.

terms.title: Secret
terms.shortDescription: A private key or password your app needs but must never expose.
terms.definition: A secret is a sensitive credential—API key, token, password—that must stay out of your code and out of public view.
terms.whenToUse: Any time you handle credentials or private keys.
aiPhrases: Make sure no secrets are hardcoded here—move them to environment variables.
examples: An API key stored as an env var, never committed to the repo.

terms.title: Domain
terms.shortDescription: The human-friendly web address people type to reach your app.
terms.definition: A domain is the name (like myapp.com) that points to your deployed app, so users don't need a raw server address.
terms.whenToUse: When giving your live app a real, memorable address.
aiPhrases: Walk me through pointing my custom domain at this deployment.
examples: Connecting myapp.com to your Vercel project.

terms.title: Rollback
terms.shortDescription: Instantly returning the live app to a previous working version.
terms.definition: A rollback reverts a deployment to an earlier known-good version, undoing a bad release fast.
terms.whenToUse: When a fresh deploy breaks production.
aiPhrases: This deploy broke the site—how do I roll back to the last working version right now?
examples: Reverting to yesterday's deploy after a bad release.

terms.title: Build
terms.shortDescription: Packaging your code into the optimized version that runs live.
terms.definition: A build converts your source code into the bundled, optimized files that actually get served; a failed build blocks deployment.
terms.whenToUse: When a deploy fails "at build" or you run it locally to check.
aiPhrases: My build is failing—read the build output and tell me the exact cause.
examples: Running `npm run build` before pushing to catch errors.

buckets.title: Landing page words
buckets.description: The plain-English fundamentals of a landing page that earns the click.

terms.title: Hero
terms.shortDescription: The first thing visitors see: headline, one line of support, and the main button.
terms.definition: The hero is the top section of the page; it should say what you offer and what to do next without scrolling.
terms.whenToUse: Always—it's your first impression.
aiPhrases: Write a hero with a clear headline, one supporting line, and a single obvious button.
examples: "Build landing pages in hours" + subline + a "Start free" button.

terms.title: Primary button (CTA)
terms.shortDescription: The one main action you want visitors to take.
terms.definition: The primary call-to-action is the single most important button—make it stand out and use an action word.
terms.whenToUse: On every page; repeat it where interest peaks.
aiPhrases: Give me three button labels that pair an action verb with the benefit.
examples: "Start the free trial" instead of "Submit."

terms.title: Value props
terms.shortDescription: A few punchy reasons your thing is worth it.
terms.definition: Value propositions are short, benefit-led statements that show how you deliver on the main promise.
terms.whenToUse: Right after the hero, to build the case.
aiPhrases: Turn these features into three benefit-led value props, each with proof.
examples: "Cut build time from weeks to hours."

terms.title: Social proof
terms.shortDescription: Evidence that other people trust you—logos, reviews, numbers.
terms.definition: Social proof reassures visitors by showing real customers, testimonials, or usage stats.
terms.whenToUse: Near the hero or just before the main button.
aiPhrases: Suggest social proof I could add and where to place it for the most reassurance.
examples: "Trusted by 4,000 founders" with a logo strip.

terms.title: Visual hierarchy
terms.shortDescription: Using size and contrast so the eye knows what to read first.
terms.definition: Visual hierarchy guides attention with type, spacing, and contrast—from headline to support to button.
terms.whenToUse: When a page feels flat or "everything shouts."
aiPhrases: Improve the visual hierarchy so the headline and main button clearly stand out.
examples: A big bold headline, quieter subtext, and a high-contrast button.

terms.title: Message match
terms.shortDescription: The page echoes the ad or link that brought the visitor.
terms.definition: Message match means the headline and look mirror what the visitor clicked, so they feel they're in the right place.
terms.whenToUse: When running ads or campaigns to a specific page.
aiPhrases: Rewrite this headline to match the ad copy that sends traffic here.
examples: The ad says "3-hour teardown"; the page headline repeats it.

terms.title: Friction reducers
terms.shortDescription: Small reassurances that make saying yes feel easy.
terms.definition: Friction reducers are microcopy, trust badges, and short forms that lower the perceived effort or risk of acting.
terms.whenToUse: Right at the decision point, near the button or form.
aiPhrases: Add friction reducers near this form so signing up feels low-risk.
examples: "No credit card needed" beside the signup button.

terms.title: Above the fold
terms.shortDescription: What shows before anyone scrolls.
terms.definition: Above the fold is the first screenful; it should answer what it is, who it's for, and how to start.
terms.whenToUse: When prioritizing what must be seen immediately.
aiPhrases: What belongs above the fold here so a first-time visitor instantly gets it?
examples: Headline, subhead, proof, and button all visible without scrolling.
